title: Where delirium screening fails on a geriatric medicine ward: a 12-week prospective observational study
subtitle: Screening completion by shift, weekday and patient group before any change to practice
statement: Ward policy requires a 4-item rapid delirium screen within 12 hours of arrival and every shift for patients aged 65 or over, but a one-week check found about half of expected screens documented and very few at night. It is not known where screening fails, for which patients, or whether documented screens were actually performed. A 12-week prospective observational study will measure completion per eligible patient-shift and the time from a positive screen to medical review, without changing practice.
whoAffected: Older inpatients on a 28-bed geriatric medicine ward, especially people with dementia or sensory loss who are at the highest risk of delirium; their families; ward nurses on all shifts; and the geriatricians who act on positive screens.
whatHurts: Undetected delirium leads to falls, longer stays, distress for families and discharge to care homes. Screens that are ticked without being done give false reassurance, and positive screens that are not acted on waste the effort of screening.
currentPractice: Nurses record the screen in the nursing notes each shift; there is no routine measurement of completion, no check that recorded screens were performed, and no fixed route for escalating a positive screen.
whyNow: The June check showed about half of expected screens documented, the geriatricians want a basis for choosing an improvement, and a research nurse is funded for 12 weeks from October.
constraints: The research nurse is funded at 0.4 FTE for 12 weeks only. No additional documentation or forms for ward nurses. Ward practice must not change during the observation period. Night observation is limited to two shifts a week.
patientCenteredGoal: Every older patient on the ward, including people with dementia or sensory loss, has delirium recognised early and reviewed by a doctor the same day.
summary: Problem framed as a descriptive prospective observational question about where and for whom delirium screening fails.
